extracted.intended_audience: students, practitioners, and educated general readers of architecture and architectural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Ruskin's prescriptive and descriptive criteria for what constitutes Gothic architecture: its moral/imaginative elements, formal rules (arches, gables, roofing), ornamentation (foliation, tracery, redundancy), and distinctions between schools (early/late, Italian/French).

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundance (accumulation of ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: REDUNDANCE -- the uncalculating bestowal of the wealth of its labor. A certain portion of Gothic effect depends upon accumulation of ornament; richness of work is, paradoxical as it may appear, a part of its humility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redundance can disguise the failure of the feeble and win the regard of the inattentive, but also arises from noble enthusiasm, unselfish sacrifice, and sympathy with the wealth of the material universe. It is characteristic (though not always essential) of the best Gothic; many influential buildings attain effect chiefly by this attribute. Example: cathedral fronts 'lost in the tapestry of its traceries.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointed arch in the roof proper
rubrics_metrics.description: "Gothic architecture is that which uses, if possible, the pointed arch in the roof proper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pointed arch as the principal form adopted in stone vaulting or the timbers of the roof proper is a primary formal condition for Gothic. Exceptions permitted when necessary (e.g., domestic apartments requiring flat ceilings), but where practicable the roof proper should employ pointed arches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gable as the roof-mask
rubrics_metrics.description: "Gothic architecture is that which uses ... the gable for the roof-mask."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The roof-mask (the external covering protecting the lower roof from weather) should be a gable; in cold/rainy climates the gable is the only advisable form. Wilful or conspicuous substitution of other forms (domes, Turkish, Chinese crowns) is a caprice that corrupts Gothic character — a deliberate transgression that un-Gothicizes a building in proportion to its conspicuousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: roof proper vs roof-mask
rubrics_metrics.description: Roofs are divided into roof proper (shell, vault, ceiling, internally visible) and roof-mask (protects the lower roof from weather); in most Gothic buildings there is an interval between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification and purity of Gothic depend on considering both parts: pointed arches ideally govern the roof proper; the gable governs the roof-mask. Buildings may be Gothic in walls/arches despite having different roof-proper forms; but roof-mask form is more determinative of perceived Gothic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foliation (essential character)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Foliated Architecture, which uses the pointed arch for the roof proper, and the gable for the roof-mask." Foliation is an essential character of the style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No Gothic is either good or characteristic which is not foliated either in its arches or apertures. Foliation may appear as cusped arches or in tracery; it must enter somewhere in the design, either in bearing arches or in the ornamentation above them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three generic roofing systems (lintel, round arch, gable)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three ways of bridging intervals between piers: A) the lintel; B) the round arch; C) the gable — corresponding broadly to Greek (lintel), Romanesque (round arch), and Gothic (gable) architectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three generic forms exhaust the structural ways of covering space; varieties of style are modifications of these. Use this classification to distinguish and relate architectural traditions and to judge purity/simplicity of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gable steepness rule (Gothic vs Romanesque)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic gable must have all its angles acute; Romanesque gable must have the upper angle obtuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical semicircle test: strike a semicircle on a gable's base — if the top rises above the semicircle it is Gothic; if it falls beneath it is Romanesque. Best forms are distinctly steep (Gothic) or distinctly low (Romanesque).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cusped pointed-arch form (structural optimum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all possible forms of the pointed arch (for a given weight of material), the generically cusped form (represented at 'e' in Ruskin's figure) is the strongest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cusped profiles thicken the flanks gradually to prevent inward fracture and outward failure, yielding maximum strength for given material. Though often ornamental, the cusp can have genuine structural advantage in smaller arches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foliation derived from study of vegetation (ornamental principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foliation and cusping rose from copying the beauty of leaves: on a small scale sculptors copied leaves; on a large scale designers adopted the abstract characters of leaf curvature and subdivision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foliation is not literal imitation of vegetation but the investment of architectural forms with the same characters of beauty discovered in leaves. Designers should avoid irregularity that would suggest crude imitation; keep structures simple and consistent with masonry principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale-sensitivity of cusps and tracery
rubrics_metrics.description: The structural advantage of cusps applies only on relatively small scales; very large arches cannot safely bear heavy cusps and rely instead on general masonry mass and tracery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On large spans, cusps would be too ponderous and liable to break off; such arches use mass and open tracery to achieve apparent or actual support. Apply cusped ornament prudently with respect to scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of tracery: geometric order + vegetal forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracery began as penetrations cut into stone that looked like stars from within and leaves from without; the name 'foil' applies to the lobes. Best traceries are close clusters of such forms with mouldings following their outlines — a mix of radiated leaf-forms and strict geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracery should combine vegetative pleasure with severe geometrical order and symmetry. Randomly crossing lines (Ruskin's Fig. XIX example) produce superficial 'pseudo-Gothic' effects; floral decoration and mouldings require invention or accurate copying to avoid commonplace results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: random/immoderate foliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Throwing any number of crossing lines together at random and filling openings with quatrefoils/cinquefoils will fool many into thinking the result is Gothic, but yields buildings without invention or intellectual merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mechanical or immoderate foliation that substitutes multiplicity of similar patterns for true invention. Overuse of foliation without inventive floral/figure ornament leads to ignoble, declining Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early (noble) vs Late (declining) Gothic — foliation and ornament balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Gothic: noble, inventive, progressive — uses foliation moderately and floral/figure sculpture profusely. Late Gothic: ignoble, uninventive, declining — uses foliation immoderately and floral/figure sculpture subordinately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge period/style by balance of foliated line-work vs surface sculpture. Early examples confine foliation to large simple masses and adorn cusp-areas with sculpture; late work decorates foliation itself with subordinate foliation, creating lace-like subdivision and repetition of the same idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear-Gothic (Italian) vs Surface-Gothic (French) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Linear-Gothic (Italian/Veronese): strong masonry, simple masses, broad sculptured surfaces, foliation confined to major arches. Surface-Gothic (French/Flamboyant): depends on multiplications of similar lines of tracery, lace-like cutting-through, broken masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate buildings by their tendency toward broad, strong, simple masses with sculptural relief (preferred by author) versus delicate, intricately pierced traceries that risk weak masonry. Ruskin favors the Italian ('nobler') approach for permanence and nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/imaginative elements of Gothic spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The inner spirit of Gothic architecture includes faith and aspiration, habits of philosophical investigation, accurate thought, domestic seclusion and independence, stern self-reliance, and sincere upright searching into religious truth; also naturalism, humility, enthusiasm, and unselfish sacrifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These moral and imaginative qualities inform the choice of forms and ornament: architecture should both admit aid and appeal to the rudest and most refined minds; richness, humility, and naturalistic ornamentation (e.g., foliage models) are expressions of this spirit and contribute to Gothic's moral character.
